tools.title: Cervical radiculopathy
niceRefs: NICE CKS Neck pain – cervical radiculopathy

options.label: Red flags
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Cervical MYELOPATHY (same-day/urgent neurosurgery): bilateral symptoms, gait disturbance, clumsy hands, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann's, upgoing plantars, bladder/bowel change.
2. Urgent: significant trauma, cancer history/weight loss/night pain, fever/IVDU/immunosuppression (infection), progressive motor deficit, vertebral artery symptoms (dizziness, drop attacks), age <20 or >55 with new severe pain.
3. Suspected cardiac/shoulder referral if pain not dermatomal.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Explain: most improve in 4–6 weeks, 80–90% by 3 months without surgery. Stay active; avoid collars beyond a few days.
2. Analgesia stepwise: paracetamol/NSAID (ibuprofen 400 mg tds or naproxen 500 mg bd with PPI) short course; neuropathic pain if radicular (CKS): amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrate to 25–50 mg, or gabapentin 300 mg od → tds (NG59 advises against gabapentinoids for non-radicular back pain only); short course of codeine only if severe and brief.
3. Physiotherapy: neural mobilisation, posture, strengthening; manual therapy as part of a package.
4. Imaging (MRI) only if red flags, progressive deficit, or persistent >6 weeks when intervention is being considered.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: myelopathy signs. Urgent (2 weeks): progressive weakness, intractable pain.
2. Spinal/MSK interface after 6–12 weeks of conservative care: MRI, nerve root block/epidural, or surgical decompression (ACDF) for persistent radicular pain with concordant MRI.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Neck pain — cervical radiculopathy, 2024; NICE NG59 for analgesic principles)

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Physiotherapy (quadriceps strengthening); avoid aggravating activities. Patellar taping if helpful.
2. Analgesia; refer if persistent. NICE CKS.

options.label: Initial Screening
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
History: Sleep, stress, diet, drugs. Bloods: FBC, Ferritin, U&E, TFT, HbA1c, Vit D, Bone, LFT, Coeliac screen. NICE CKS.

options.label: Suspected ME/CFS
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Persistent fatigue >3 months. Check NICE NG206 for diagnostic criteria. Do not offer LET or GET. Focus on energy management (pacing).

options.label: Acute — emergency
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. After fracture (tibia, forearm), crush, tight cast, reperfusion or anticoagulation: pain OUT OF PROPORTION, worse on passive stretch of the compartment muscles, tense swollen compartment, paraesthesia; pulses are preserved until late — do not wait for pulselessness.
2. Action: 999/immediate ED. Remove/split any cast or dressing to skin, keep limb at heart level (do not elevate above), analgesia, nil by mouth. Fasciotomy within hours prevents permanent damage.

options.label: Chronic exertional
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Runners/military: cramping tightness in a compartment after a predictable duration of exercise, resolves with rest; normal examination at rest; may have transient numbness.
2. Management: reduce provoking load, gait retraining (forefoot strike), footwear; physiotherapy. Diagnosis by intracompartmental pressure testing in sports medicine/orthopaedics; fasciotomy if conservative care fails.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute: emergency, never outpatient.
2. Chronic: routine sports medicine/orthopaedic referral; exclude popliteal artery entrapment and tibial stress injury first.

curated.by: Claude draft (BOAST 10 Diagnosis and management of compartment syndrome; NICE CKS)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Numbness/tingling in little and ring fingers, worse with elbow flexion (phone, sleeping); positive Tinel at cubital tunnel, elbow flexion test; later weakness of grip/pinch, interossei wasting, clawing (Froment's sign).
2. Differentials: C8 radiculopathy (neck pain, triceps), thoracic outlet, Guyon's canal (dorsal hand sensation spared), medial epicondylitis.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Activity modification: avoid leaning on elbow, prolonged flexion; elbow pad; night splint/towel wrap keeping elbow ≤45° flexion for 6–12 weeks.
2. Analgesia if needed: paracetamol/NSAID. Steroid injection has no proven benefit.
3. Nerve conduction studies if persistent >6–8 weeks, any motor signs, or before surgery.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Urgent hand/plastic surgery: motor weakness, muscle wasting, or constant numbness (irreversible if delayed).
2. Routine: sensory symptoms persisting >3 months despite conservative care — decompression ± transposition.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS — peripheral nerve entrapment; BSSH)

options.label: Assessment & diagnosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Clinical: Radial-side wrist/thumb pain; Finkelstein's test positive (thumb in fist, ulnar deviation reproduces pain). Tenderness over first dorsal compartment.
2. Differentiate: CMC arthritis, Wartenberg's (superficial radial nerve), intersection syndrome. NICE CKS, Local formulary.

options.label: Conservative & injection
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Conservative: Splint (thumb spica); NSAID; activity modification (avoid repetitive pinch/grasp).
2. Injection: First dorsal compartment – steroid (e.g. methylprednisolone 20–40 mg or triamcinolone) + local anaesthetic. Aseptic technique; inject into tendon sheath. Warn steroid flare (24–48 h); rest 48 h. Repeat once after 4–6 weeks if partial response. NICE CKS, Local formulary.

options.label: When to refer
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Refer hand surgery if: Symptoms persist >1 year despite injection(s) and conservative treatment; diagnostic uncertainty; or recurrence after repeated injection.
2. Do not refer within first year without adequate conservative trial. NICE CKS, Right Decisions Scotland.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Mild: Reassurance; hand therapy. Refer when contracture affects function (e.g. table-top test).
2. Treatment: Collagenase or fasciectomy. NICE CKS.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Tenderness at medial epicondyle, pain on resisted wrist flexion/pronation. Check ulnar nerve: paraesthesia ring/little finger, Tinel at cubital tunnel (co-exists in up to 50%).
2. Differentials: cubital tunnel syndrome, ulnar collateral ligament injury (throwers), C8/T1 radiculopathy.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Activity modification; topical NSAID gel; paracetamol.
2. Physiotherapy: eccentric/isometric wrist flexor–pronator loading 6–12 weeks; counterforce brace.
3. Steroid injection: short-term relief only; risk of ulnar nerve injury — specialist/USS-guided if at all.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Refer MSK/orthopaedics if >6 months, progressive ulnar neuropathy (weakness, wasting → nerve conduction studies), or instability.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Tennis elbow — medial section; BMJ Best Practice)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Fluctuant swelling over the olecranon, usually painless with full elbow movement (unlike septic arthritis where movement is restricted).
2. SEPTIC bursitis (~1/3): warmth, erythema, tenderness, overlying skin break, fever; risks — trauma, diabetes, immunosuppression, gout, RA. Aspirate for Gram stain/culture/crystals if infection or gout suspected (aseptic technique; avoid repeated aspiration).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Aseptic: avoid pressure/leaning, compression (elastic sleeve), ice, NSAID (ibuprofen 400 mg tds or naproxen 500 mg bd with food) 1–2 weeks; aspiration ± corticosteroid injection (methylprednisolone 20–40 mg) only if infection excluded and persistent — risk of skin atrophy/infection.
2. Septic: aspirate (send fluid), then flucloxacillin 500 mg–1 g qds for 7 days (clarithromycin 500 mg bd if penicillin-allergic; review MRSA risk); review at 48 h; extend course if slow response.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day orthopaedics/ED: systemically unwell, spreading cellulitis, immunosuppressed, failure to improve at 48 h on antibiotics, suspected joint involvement.
2. Routine orthopaedics: recurrent/persistent aseptic bursitis >8–12 weeks (bursectomy).

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Olecranon bursitis, 2024)

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Eccentric exercises; avoid aggravating activities. NSAID/paracetamol. Consider steroid injection if persistent.
2. Refer if refractory. NICE CKS, NG124.

options.label: Diagnosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Chronic widespread pain ≥3 months (ACR 2016 criteria: widespread pain index + symptom severity), fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive symptoms ('fibro fog'); tender points no longer required.
2. Make a POSITIVE diagnosis in primary care and explain it — avoid repeated investigation. Baseline to exclude mimics: FBC, ESR/CRP, U&E, LFT, calcium, CK, TSH, HbA1c, vitamin D, ± ferritin, coeliac serology. Normal inflammatory markers expected.
3. Screen for and treat comorbid depression, anxiety, sleep apnoea, IBS.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Non-drug first (EULAR strong recommendation): education on central sensitisation; graded aerobic exercise (walking, aquatic) built up slowly; sleep hygiene; CBT or ACT; pain management programme; social prescribing/peer support (Versus Arthritis).
2. Drugs (modest benefit, trial 4–6 weeks, stop if no benefit): amitriptyline 10 mg at night, increase by 10 mg weekly to 25–50 mg; OR duloxetine 30 mg od → 60 mg (off-label, helpful if depression); OR pregabalin 75 mg bd → 150–225 mg bd (controlled drug, dependence risk — NICE NG193 advises against starting gabapentinoids for primary chronic pain; use only if diagnosis is fibromyalgia with specialist-level rationale).
3. Do NOT start opioids, NSAIDs, benzodiazepines, or paracetamol for fibromyalgia pain (NG193). Deprescribe existing opioids gradually.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Rheumatology only for diagnostic doubt (inflammatory features, raised markers, synovitis).
2. Community pain service / pain management programme for multidisciplinary support; IAPT/talking therapies for CBT; occupational health if work affected.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE NG193 Chronic pain 2021; EULAR fibromyalgia 2016; NICE CKS)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Lateral deviation of great toe with medial prominence, pain from shoe pressure, bursitis, transfer metatarsalgia, lesser toe deformity. Weight-bearing X-ray only if surgery considered.
2. Check for hallux rigidus (OA — pain on dorsiflexion), gout, RA, diabetic/neuropathic foot (ulceration risk).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Footwear: wide, deep toe box, low heel, soft upper; bunion pads/toe spacers for comfort (do not correct deformity); orthoses if flat foot.
2. Analgesia: paracetamol; topical or oral NSAID short course for bursitis flares.
3. Diabetic/neuropathic foot: podiatry early to prevent ulceration.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Orthopaedic foot & ankle referral for pain and functional limitation despite 6 months conservative care, ulceration/skin breakdown, or progressive lesser-toe deformity. Surgery (scarf/Akin, Lapidus, minimally invasive) is NOT for cosmesis alone; warn of 6–12 week recovery and recurrence risk.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS — bunions; BOFAS)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Burning/shooting forefoot pain radiating to toes, 'pebble in shoe', worse in tight shoes, relieved by removing shoe; 3rd/4th web space commonest; Mulder's click on squeeze. Women 40–60.
2. Differentials: metatarsal stress fracture, MTP synovitis/plantar plate tear (2nd MTP), Freiberg's, bursitis. USS confirms if needed.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Wide, low-heeled shoes; metatarsal dome/pad or orthoses; weight loss; activity modification; paracetamol/ibuprofen 400 mg tds prn.
2. Persistent at 3 months: USS-guided corticosteroid injection (methylprednisolone 20–40 mg) — relief in ~50% at 3 months; max 2.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Podiatry/MSK for orthoses and injection. Orthopaedic foot & ankle if failure after 6 months conservative care: neurectomy or radiofrequency ablation.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS — forefoot pain; NICE IPG; BOFAS)

options.label: Freezing Stage (Painful / Inflammatory)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN (Consultant Grade):
1. Primary Intervention: US-guided Intra-articular Corticosteroid Injection (40mg Triamcinolone). Superior to PT in early stage.
2. Analgesia: Scheduled NSAIDs (e.g. Naproxen 500mg bd with PPI) + Paracetamol/Codeine as rescue.
3. Physiotherapy: Gentle active-assisted ROM within pain-free limits. Avoid aggressive stretching in inflammatory phase.
4. Education: Natural history (12-24 month duration). NICE CKS / BESS Guidelines.

options.label: Frozen Stage (Stiff / Fibrotic)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN (Consultant Grade):
1. Hydrodilatation: Consider high-volume image-guided distension (Injecting 20-30ml saline + steroid) to disrupt capsular adhesions.
2. Physiotherapy: Home Exercise Programme (HEP) focusing on external rotation and abduction. 4-5 times daily.
3. Monitoring: Review for secondary rotator cuff disuse atrophy. NICE CKS / BESS Guidelines.

options.label: Refractory / Severe Functional Impairment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN (Consultant Grade):
1. Surgical Referral: Orthopaedic review for Manipulation Under Anaesthesia (MUA) or Arthroscopic Capsular Release (ACR).
2. Indication: Failure of 6 months conservative management with significant impact on sleep/QoL.
3. Post-Op: Mandatory immediate intensive PT to maintain surgical gains.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Smooth, firm, transilluminable cystic swelling, dorsal (70%) or volar wrist, flexor sheath (pea-sized at finger base) or DIP (mucous cyst with nail ridging). Usually painless; may fluctuate in size.
2. Volar ganglion: check radial artery (Allen's test) — surgery/aspiration risk. Imaging (USS) only if diagnosis unclear (solid lump, fixed, rapid growth → 2WW sarcoma pathway).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Reassure: benign, ~50% resolve spontaneously within 1–2 years; leave alone unless painful, limiting function or cosmetically distressing after discussion. Do not 'bash with a Bible'.
2. Aspiration (large-bore needle, ± steroid) — recurrence ~50%; avoid for volar wrist ganglia (artery) unless USS-guided.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Hand surgery: persistent pain, nerve compression symptoms, functional limitation, recurrent after aspiration, mucous cyst with nail deformity — excision (recurrence 10–20%). Local commissioning may require pain/function criteria (procedures of limited clinical value).

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS — ganglion; BSSH)

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Reassurance; many resolve. Avoid aspiration (high recurrence). Refer if symptomatic or diagnostic uncertainty. NICE CKS.

steps.question: Giant cell arteritis — treat as emergency

options.label: Recognise
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Age ≥50 with new temporal/occipital headache, scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication, visual symptoms (amaurosis, diplopia, blur), PMR symptoms, fever/weight loss, thickened tender non-pulsatile temporal artery.
2. Bloods SAME DAY: ESR, CRP, FBC (thrombocytosis), LFT (raised ALP). Normal ESR/CRP does not exclude GCA if clinical suspicion is high. Do NOT delay steroids for results.

options.label: Immediate treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. No visual symptoms: start prednisolone 40–60 mg once daily immediately (same day).
2. Visual symptoms or jaw claudication: 60 mg prednisolone and SAME-DAY ophthalmology/ED referral (IV methylprednisolone 500 mg–1 g for 3 days in secondary care). Vision loss is usually irreversible — minutes matter.
3. Add: gastroprotection (lansoprazole 30 mg od); bone protection (alendronic acid 70 mg weekly + calcium/vitamin D); aspirin 75 mg not routinely (BSR 2020) unless other indication; steroid card.
4. Ensure specialist review within 3 working days (fast-track GCA pathway where available) for temporal artery ultrasound/biopsy — steroids should not be stopped while awaiting confirmation.

options.label: Ongoing
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Specialist-led taper over 12–18 months (e.g. to 20 mg by 3 months, 10 mg by 6 months); relapse → increase. Tocilizumab (NICE TA518) for relapsing/refractory disease — rheumatology.
2. GP monitoring: BP, glucose, weight, mood, infection; relapse symptoms; long-term aortic imaging per specialist.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Giant cell arteritis, 2024; BSR 2020)

options.label: Acute attack
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
NSAID (e.g. naproxen) + PPI, or colchicine 500 mcg bd–qd (max 6 mg per attack), or prednisolone 30 mg 3–5 days. Start within 24 h. NICE NG219.

options.label: Urate-lowering (recurrent or tophi)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Allopurinol 100 mg daily, titrate to target sUA <300 µmol/L. Prophylaxis: colchicine or NSAID for first 6 months. NICE NG219.

options.label: When to refer / renal / prophylaxis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Refer rheumatology: Diagnostic uncertainty, recurrent despite urate-lowering, tophi, CKD. Reduce allopurinol dose if eGFR <60; avoid in severe CKD without specialist advice.
2. Prophylaxis during urate-lowering: colchicine 500 mcg bd or NSAID for up to 6 months. NICE NG219, CKS.

options.label: Acute attack
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
NSAID (e.g. naproxen) + PPI, or colchicine 500 mcg bd–qd (max 6 mg per attack), or prednisolone 30 mg 3–5 days. Start within 24 h. NICE NG219.

2. Prophylaxis during urate-lowering: colchicine 500 mcg bd or NSAID for up to 6 months. NICE NG219, CKS.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Painless palmar nodules/cords, ring and little finger commonest; measure MCP and PIP flexion contracture; table-top test (cannot lay palm flat).
2. Risk: family history, Northern European, diabetes, alcohol, smoking, epilepsy drugs. Note ectopic disease (Garrod's pads, plantar fascia, Peyronie's).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Nodules without contracture: reassure, no treatment; splints, NSAIDs, physiotherapy and steroid injection do NOT alter progression.
2. Advise on smoking/alcohol; optimise diabetes. Explain variable progression; review if function declines.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Refer hand surgery when: MCP contracture ≥30°, ANY PIP contracture, positive table-top test, rapidly progressive disease, functional impairment, or first-web/thumb involvement.
2. Options: needle fasciotomy (quick, higher recurrence), limited fasciectomy (standard), dermofasciectomy for recurrence. Collagenase (Xiapex) withdrawn from UK market 2020.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Dupuytren's disease, 2024; BSSH)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Catching/locking of the finger in flexion with painful nodule at A1 pulley (palm, MCP crease). Grade: I pain, II catching, III locking (releases with help), IV fixed.
2. Associations: diabetes (check HbA1c if not known), RA, carpal tunnel, Dupuytren's. Children: congenital trigger thumb → hand surgery.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Mild: activity modification, avoid repetitive gripping; paracetamol/ibuprofen; night splint holding MCP in extension for 6 weeks (resolves ~50%).
2. Corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath at A1 pulley (e.g. methylprednisolone 20–40 mg + lidocaine): effective in ~60–90%; second injection if recurs; lower success in diabetes. Warn of skin/fat atrophy and transient glucose rise.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Hand surgery referral: locked digit (grade IV), failure of 2 injections, multiple digits, diabetes with poor response, children. Percutaneous or open A1 pulley release — >95% success.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Trigger finger, 2024; BSSH)

tools.title: Hip – trochanteric bursitis
niceRefs: NICE CKS Greater trochanteric pain syndrome

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Lateral hip pain worse lying on that side, climbing stairs, standing on one leg; tenderness over greater trochanter; pain on resisted abduction/30-second single-leg stand. Women 40–60, often with low back pain or knee OA.
2. Exclude: hip OA (groin pain, restricted internal rotation → X-ray), lumbar radiculopathy L4/5, stress fracture femoral neck (runners, osteoporosis → urgent), septic bursitis (rare, unwell).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Education and load management: avoid lying on the affected side (pillow between knees), avoid crossing legs, sitting low, hanging on one hip; weight loss if indicated.
2. Analgesia: paracetamol; ibuprofen 400 mg tds/naproxen 500 mg bd short course; topical NSAID.
3. Physiotherapy: progressive gluteal (abductor) strengthening ≥8–12 weeks — better long-term outcomes than injection (LEAP trial).
4. Corticosteroid injection (methylprednisolone 40 mg + lidocaine, to point of maximal tenderness) for short-term relief if severe; max 2–3/year.
5. Persistent: ESWT via MSK service.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. MSK/orthopaedics if no improvement after 3–6 months of exercise therapy ± injection; USS/MRI for gluteal tendon tear.
2. Urgent: suspected femoral neck stress fracture or inability to weight-bear.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Greater trochanteric pain syndrome, 2024)

tools.title: Inflammatory, infective and regional MSK conditions – spondyloarthritis, reactive arthritis, vasculitis, osteomyelitis, CRPS and others
niceRefs: RCP Complex regional pain syndrome guidelines 2018

options.label: Spondyloarthritis and reactive arthritis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Axial SpA (NG65): low back pain >3 months starting <45 years with ≥4 of — onset <35, waking in second half of night, buttock pain, improves with movement, improves within 48 h of NSAIDs, first-degree relative with SpA, current/past arthritis/enthesitis/psoriasis → refer rheumatology (do not wait for X-ray changes; HLA-B27 and MRI arranged by specialist). Treat: NSAID at full dose (naproxen 500 mg bd) for 2–4 weeks with PPI, physio/exercise (NASS), smoking cessation; biologics (anti-TNF, IL-17, JAK) for persistent high disease activity (BASDAI ≥4) via rheumatology.
2. Peripheral SpA (psoriatic, IBD-related, reactive): dactylitis ('sausage digit'), enthesitis (Achilles, plantar), asymmetric oligoarthritis, nail changes → rheumatology (urgent if ≥3 joints or synovitis — early DMARD window).
3. Reactive arthritis: 1–4 weeks after GI (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, Yersinia) or GU (Chlamydia) infection; asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis ± conjunctivitis/urethritis/keratoderma. Tests: CRP, FBC, HLA-B27, STI screen (NAAT; treat chlamydia and partners), stool culture if diarrhoea, aspirate if septic doubt. NSAID (naproxen 500 mg bd) + PPI; intra-articular steroid; sulfasalazine/methotrexate if >3–6 months (rheumatology); most settle in 3–12 months; recurrence in HLA-B27+.

options.label: Vasculitis — ANCA and IgA
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. ANCA-associated (GPA/Wegener's, MPA, EGPA): consider in adults with unexplained systemic symptoms + any of: persistent sinusitis/crusting/epistaxis, haemoptysis, palpable purpura, mononeuritis multiplex, red eye/scleritis, haematuria/proteinuria/rising creatinine, late-onset asthma + eosinophilia (EGPA). Tests SAME DAY: urine dip + protein:creatinine ratio, U&E, FBC, CRP/ESR, ANCA (PR3/MPO), chest X-ray. Active urinary sediment or rising creatinine or lung haemorrhage = EMERGENCY → same-day renal/rheumatology; otherwise urgent rheumatology (within 1–2 weeks). Treatment: high-dose steroids + rituximab or cyclophosphamide induction, then maintenance (specialist); GP — PJP prophylaxis awareness, bone protection, vaccination, infection vigilance, BP.
2. IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura): children 3–10 (adults rarer, worse renal outcomes) — palpable purpura on legs/buttocks, arthralgia, abdominal pain, haematuria. Check BP, urinalysis, U&E, FBC (platelets normal — distinguishes from ITP/meningococcus), clotting. Usually self-limiting 4–6 weeks: paracetamol/ibuprofen (avoid NSAID if renal involvement); refer same day if severe abdominal pain (intussusception), GI bleeding, nephrotic/nephritic (proteinuria >1 g, hypertension, rising creatinine), testicular pain. Follow-up: BP + urinalysis weekly for 1 month, 2-weekly to 3 months, then at 6 and 12 months; persistent haematuria/proteinuria → paediatric nephrology.

options.label: Bone and joint infection, AVN, CRPS
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Osteomyelitis: localised bone pain, swelling, fever (may be absent in diabetic foot/vertebral); risk — diabetes, open fracture, prosthesis, IVDU, immunosuppression, sickle cell (Salmonella). Tests: FBC, CRP/ESR, blood cultures ×2, X-ray (changes late, 10–14 days), MRI. Diabetic foot with probe-to-bone positive/ulcer >2 cm → same-day diabetic foot MDT. Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis (back pain + fever/raised CRP ± neurology) → same-day admission (MRI, cultures, 6 weeks IV/oral antibiotics; epidural abscess = emergency). Do NOT start antibiotics before cultures unless septic. Soft-tissue infection (cellulitis/abscess) → see Dermatology cellulitis tool; necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus, systemic toxicity) = 999.
2. Avascular necrosis (hip): groin pain, often night, in steroids (≥20 mg prednisolone for weeks), alcohol excess, sickle cell, SLE, HIV, chemotherapy, divers; X-ray may be normal early → MRI; urgent orthopaedics (core decompression before collapse; THR after); stop/reduce steroids where possible; bisphosphonates not proven.
3. Complex regional pain syndrome (Budapest criteria): continuing regional pain disproportionate after injury/surgery, with sensory (allodynia), vasomotor (colour/temperature), sudomotor/oedema, and motor/trophic changes. EARLY recognition matters: start physiotherapy/OT immediately (graded motor imagery, mirror therapy, desensitisation, keep moving), amitriptyline 10–75 mg nocte or gabapentin/pregabalin (NICE CG173), short course prednisolone 30–40 mg tapered over 2–3 weeks in early CRPS (specialist), bisphosphonate (pamidronate/neridronate — pain clinic), avoid immobilisation and repeated surgery; refer pain clinic within 1–2 months if not improving (RCP). Psychological support; sleep; return-to-work planning.

options.label: Regional conditions — labral tear, patellar tendinopathy, AC joint, metatarsalgia, sarcoid
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Hip labral tear/femoroacetabular impingement: young active adult, anterior groin pain/clicking/catching, positive FADIR test; X-ray (cam/pincer morphology), MR arthrogram via specialist; physiotherapy (hip stabiliser strengthening, avoid deep flexion/pivoting) 3 months; image-guided steroid injection; refer young-adult hip surgeon for arthroscopy if persistent and no OA (NICE IPG408); FAI with established OA → OA pathway.
2. Patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee): inferior pole pain on loading; relative rest, isometric then heavy slow resistance/decline-squat eccentric programme 12 weeks, patellar strap, avoid steroid injection into tendon; ESWT; refer if >6 months.
3. AC joint arthritis/osteoarthritis: pain at the top of the shoulder, high-arc (>150°) pain, cross-body adduction positive, tender over ACJ; X-ray; activity modification, NSAID, ACJ steroid injection (small volume, USS-guided ideally), refer orthopaedics for distal clavicle excision if persistent.
4. Metatarsalgia: forefoot pain under metatarsal heads — causes: high heels, hallux valgus transfer, plantar plate tear (2nd MTP — drawer test), Morton's neuroma, stress fracture, Freiberg's (adolescent 2nd MT head — X-ray), RA (check), diabetes/neuropathy; footwear (wide, low heel, cushioned), metatarsal dome/orthoses, calf stretches, NSAID, weight; podiatry; refer if persistent >6 months or plantar plate rupture (progressive toe deviation).
5. Sarcoid arthropathy: Löfgren's syndrome (acute ankle periarthritis + erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy) — self-limiting, NSAIDs, chest X-ray, calcium, ACE; refer respiratory/rheumatology; chronic sarcoid arthritis → rheumatology (methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine).

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE NG65 Spondyloarthritis 2017; NICE CKS; BSR ANCA vasculitis 2014/2024; BSR reactive arthritis; RCP CRPS 2018; BOAST; BNF)

options.label: Medical management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Antiplatelet (clopidogrel 75 mg or aspirin). Statin. Treat BP and diabetes. Supervised exercise.
2. Refer vascular if limiting symptoms or critical ischaemia. NICE NG147.

options.label: Benign Lumps (Indications for GP Surgery)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Criteria: Symptomatic (pain, inflammation, interference with function). 
2. Lipomas: Usually only if >5cm or rapidly growing (refer for US first to exclude sarcoma).
3. Sebaceous Cysts: Excise if recurrently infected (wait for infection to settle first).
4. Exclusions: Cosmetic removal is generally not routinely publicly funded.

options.label: Red Flags (Refer to 2WW / Plastic Surgery)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Changing Naevi: Refer to 2WW Dermatology.
2. Irregular, fixed, or hard masses: Urgent referral.
3. Note: Never excise a lesion where malignancy is suspected in primary care minor surgery clinic.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. ACL: pivot/landing injury, audible pop, immediate swelling (haemarthrosis within 1–2 h), instability; Lachman most sensitive. 50% have meniscal injury too.
2. MCL: valgus force, medial pain, laxity at 30° flexion — grade I–III. PCL: dashboard injury, posterior sag. Multi-ligament/dislocation → vascular check.
3. X-ray per Ottawa rules; Segond fracture on X-ray = ACL until proven otherwise.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute: rest, ice, compression, elevation, crutches; paracetamol + ibuprofen 400 mg tds; hinged brace for MCL grade II–III.
2. MCL grade I–II: physiotherapy, early range of movement, return to sport 2–8 weeks. Isolated PCL: physiotherapy quadriceps-focused.
3. ACL: structured physiotherapy (prehabilitation) for all; reconstruction decision with orthopaedics based on instability, age, activity and associated meniscal injury.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day ED/orthopaedics: haemarthrosis, suspected dislocation or multi-ligament injury, neurovascular compromise, locked knee.
2. Urgent orthopaedic (within 2 weeks): suspected ACL rupture, MCL grade III, PCL with instability — MRI arranged by secondary care or MSK interface.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Knee pain — assessment; BOAST)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Twisting injury with delayed swelling (hours), joint-line tenderness, pain on McMurray/Thessaly, ± locking or giving way. Degenerative tears in >40s often without clear injury.
2. Ottawa knee rules for X-ray after trauma: age ≥55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, cannot flex to 90°, cannot weight-bear 4 steps.
3. Immediate large haemarthrosis → think ACL/fracture (see Knee – ligament).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Degenerative tear or tear with OA: treat as OA — exercise, weight management, paracetamol/topical NSAID, physiotherapy for ≥3 months. NICE NG226: do NOT refer for arthroscopic lavage/debridement for OA; arthroscopy only for true mechanical locking.
2. Acute traumatic tear in young/active patient: protect, ice, analgesia (ibuprofen 400 mg tds), physiotherapy; early orthopaedic opinion if mechanical symptoms (repairable tears are time-sensitive).

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day/urgent: true locked knee (cannot fully extend), suspected bucket-handle tear, haemarthrosis.
2. Orthopaedics/MSK with MRI: young patient with mechanical symptoms, or failure of 3 months physiotherapy. Over 50 without locking: X-ray and OA pathway first; MRI rarely changes management.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE NG226 Osteoarthritis 2022; NICE CKS Knee pain — assessment)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diffuse anterior/retropatellar pain worse on stairs (down > up), squatting, prolonged sitting ('theatre sign'); crepitus; no effusion or locking. Common in adolescents and runners.
2. No imaging unless red flags, trauma, effusion, locking, or failure to improve at 6–12 weeks. Differentials: patellar tendinopathy (inferior pole), Osgood–Schlatter (tibial tuberosity, adolescent), plica, OA (>50), referred hip (SUFE/Perthes in children — examine the hip).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Education; relative rest from aggravating load, then graded return.
2. Physiotherapy: quadriceps (VMO) and hip abductor/external rotator strengthening ≥12 weeks is the core treatment; patellar taping for short-term relief; foot orthoses if pronation.
3. Analgesia short term: paracetamol; ibuprofen 400 mg tds prn. Avoid steroid injection.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Physiotherapy at diagnosis. MSK/orthopaedics only if not improving after 6 months of supervised rehabilitation, recurrent patellar instability/dislocation, or diagnostic uncertainty (MRI).

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Knee pain — assessment, 2024; BJSM consensus)

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Rest; ice; avoid kneeling. Aspiration if swollen; exclude infection (aspirate for culture if hot/red). Avoid steroid if septic. Refer if septic or recurrent.
2. CKS Knee pain.

options.label: No red flags
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Advise stay active; paracetamol + NSAID short-term. Consider manual therapy. Do not offer imaging. Review at 6 weeks. NICE NG59.

options.label: Red flags (cauda equina, fracture, infection)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Cauda equina: emergency referral. Consider fracture if trauma/steroids; infection if fever. MRI if nerve root compression suspected for surgical option. NICE NG59.

options.label: Sciatica / nerve root
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Advise stay active; analgesia. Consider pregabalin/gabapentin for neuropathic pain if significant.
2. Refer if severe or progressive; consider MRI for surgical option if not improving after 6 weeks. NICE NG59.

options.label: Safety net
options.guidance: SAFETY: Reattend if new leg weakness, saddle numbness, urinary retention, or fever with back pain. Cauda equina: emergency. NICE NG59.

options.label: Principles
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Paracetamol first; add NSAID if no contraindication (short-term; PPI if GI risk). Opioid only if severe; lowest dose, shortest duration (e.g. 3 days); avoid codeine where possible. NICE NG193.
2. Red flags: fracture, infection, cauda equina, ischaemia – urgent. NICE NG59.

options.label: When to refer
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Emergency: cauda equina, cord compression, septic arthritis, acute abdomen. 2WW: suspected malignancy, red flags. Routine: persistent after expected healing. NICE NG12, NG59.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Wider footwear; metatarsal pad. Steroid injection. Refer if refractory for surgical opinion. NICE CKS.

options.label: Red Flags (Cauda Equina / Malignancy)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica, night pain, weight loss, history of cancer. Urgent same-day referral/A&E. NICE NG59.

options.label: Stable / Spondylosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Keep active. NSAIDs (regular) for flare. Physiotherapy referral. Avoid imaging in non-specific low back pain. Reassure if no neurology. NICE NG59.

options.label: Headache (migraine / tension / red flags)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Migraine: triptan + NSAID at onset; prophylaxis if ≥2/month (propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate). Tension: paracetamol/NSAID; avoid medication-overuse. Red flags: thunderclap – 999; new ≥50y or progressive – 2WW. NICE NG150, NG12.

options.label: Seizure / epilepsy / TIA / stroke
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. First seizure: refer. Epilepsy: drug review; driving (DVLA). TIA: aspirin 300 mg then 75 mg; refer same-day. Stroke: 999. NICE NG217, NG128.

options.label: Cranial nerve / neuropathy
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Bell's palsy: steroid within 72 h; eye care. Trigeminal neuralgia: carbamazepine; refer for MRI. Peripheral neuropathy: B12, glucose, thyroid; refer if cause unclear. Myasthenia/MND: refer. NICE NG150, CKS.

options.label: Red Flags (Cauda Equina / Malignancy)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica, night pain, weight loss, history of cancer. Urgent same-day referral/A&E. NICE NG59.

options.label: Stable / Spondylosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Keep active. NSAIDs (regular) for flare. Physiotherapy referral. Avoid imaging in non-specific low back pain. Reassure if no neurology. NICE NG59.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Exclude septic (aspirate if red/hot). Rest, padding. Aspiration if large; avoid steroid if septic. NICE CKS.

options.label: Shoulder
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Look (asymmetry, wasting); Feel (ACJ, SCJ, humerus); Move (Active/Passive: Abd, Flex, Rot). Tests: Hawkins-Kennedy (impingement), Empty Can (Supraspinatus).

options.label: Knee
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Look (effusion, alignment); Feel (joint line tenderness, temperature); Move (Active/Passive Flex/Ext). Tests: Lachman (ACL), McMurray (Meniscus), Patellar Tap (effusion).

options.label: Hip
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Look (gait, Trendelenburg); Feel (greater trochanter); Move (Flex, Int/Ext Rotation). Special: Thomas test (flexion contracture).

options.label: Spine (Back/Neck)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:

tools.title: Osteoarthritis – hip, knee, hand, shoulder, ankle

options.label: Diagnosis — no imaging needed
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG226: diagnose clinically WITHOUT X-ray if age ≥45, activity-related joint pain, and morning stiffness ≤30 min (or none). Image only if atypical (rapid worsening, hot joint, night pain, trauma, age <45) — X-ray severity does not match symptoms.
2. Exclude: inflammatory arthritis (prolonged stiffness, swelling, raised CRP, RF/anti-CCP → rheumatology), gout/pseudogout, septic arthritis (hot, unwell — same day), referred pain (hip → knee; spine → hip), avascular necrosis (steroids, alcohol, sickle), stress fracture.
3. Assess: function, sleep, mood, falls, work, BMI, comorbidities limiting drug choice; use shared decision tools.

options.label: Core treatment and drugs
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. CORE (all patients, NG226): therapeutic exercise — muscle strengthening + aerobic, supervised initially (physio, ESCAPE-pain, Versus Arthritis programmes), 'hurt not harm' message; weight loss if overweight (≥10% gives large benefit); education and self-management plan; appropriate footwear, walking stick in contralateral hand, hand splints for thumb-base OA.
2. Drugs (adjuncts only): topical NSAID (ibuprofen 5%/diclofenac 1% gel tds–qds) FIRST for knee/hand; oral NSAID (ibuprofen 400 mg tds, naproxen 250–500 mg bd) at lowest dose for shortest time with PPI; paracetamol and weak opioids NOT routinely (NG226 — minimal benefit) — paracetamol only short-term infrequent use; do not offer strong opioids, glucosamine, chondroitin, acupuncture, arthroscopic lavage.
3. Intra-articular corticosteroid (methylprednisolone 40 mg/triamcinolone 40 mg ± lidocaine) for short-term relief (2–10 weeks) when other options failed or to enable exercise; not more than every 3 months; hyaluronic acid not recommended.
4. Sleep/mood: CBT-informed approaches, pain management programme; duloxetine not recommended by NICE for OA (off-label option in some pathways).

options.label: Joint-specific points and referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Knee: patellofemoral vs tibiofemoral; valgus/varus brace or insoles may help; degenerative meniscal tear = OA (no arthroscopy). Hip: groin pain, limited internal rotation; stress fracture of femoral neck in osteoporotic/runner → urgent. Hand: DIP (Heberden's), PIP (Bouchard's), thumb CMC — splint, topical NSAID, steroid injection to CMC. Shoulder (glenohumeral): loss of external rotation, crepitus; X-ray distinguishes from frozen shoulder; physio, injection, arthroplasty if severe. Ankle: usually post-traumatic; rocker-sole shoes, ankle-foot orthosis, injection, arthrodesis/arthroplasty via foot & ankle surgeon.
2. Refer for joint replacement (NG226): symptoms substantially affecting quality of life AND core treatments tried — do NOT withhold referral on grounds of age, BMI, smoking or comorbidities alone (optimise but refer); use Oxford hip/knee score locally. Give realistic expectations: 80–90% satisfied, 10–15% persistent pain after TKR; recovery 3–6 months.
3. Review: within 12 months if on NSAIDs/drugs, otherwise as needed; multimorbidity — review analgesic burden annually.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE NG226 Osteoarthritis 2022; NICE CKS Osteoarthritis 2024; BNF)

options.label: Osteoporosis – fracture / DEXA
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. FRAX; DEXA if indicated. Calcium + vitamin D. First-line: oral bisphosphonate (alendronate/risedronate); ensure correct administration. Consider IV zoledronate if oral not tolerated. NICE NG146, CKS.

options.label: Osteoporosis – denosumab / teriparatide
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Denosumab: 6-monthly SC; do not miss doses (rebound fracture risk). Monitor calcium/vitamin D. Teriparatide: specialist; limited duration. NICE NG146, CKS.

options.label: Osteomalacia / Paget's
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Osteomalacia: vitamin D repletion; treat cause. Paget's: refer or bisphosphonate per specialist. NICE CKS.

options.label: Osteoporosis – fracture / DEXA
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. FRAX; DEXA if indicated. Calcium + vitamin D. First-line: oral bisphosphonate (alendronate/risedronate); ensure correct administration. Consider IV zoledronate if oral not tolerated. NICE NG146, CKS.

options.label: Osteoporosis – denosumab / teriparatide
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Denosumab: 6-monthly SC; do not miss doses (rebound fracture risk). Monitor calcium/vitamin D. Teriparatide: specialist; limited duration. NICE NG146, CKS.

options.label: Osteomalacia / Paget's
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Osteomalacia: vitamin D repletion; treat cause. Paget's: refer or bisphosphonate per specialist. NICE CKS.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Clinical diagnosis: heel pain worst on first steps in the morning or after rest, tender at medial calcaneal tubercle. Imaging not routinely needed.
2. Differentials: calcaneal stress fracture (pain on squeeze test, runners), Sever's disease (child 8–14), tarsal tunnel/S1 radiculopathy (paraesthesia), fat pad atrophy, spondyloarthritis (young, bilateral, inflammatory back pain, psoriasis/IBD).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Rest from aggravating activity; weight loss if BMI raised; supportive footwear with cushioned heel; avoid barefoot on hard floors.
2. Plantar fascia and calf stretches 2–3× daily; ice after activity.
3. Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g qds prn; ibuprofen 400 mg tds prn with food (or topical ibuprofen gel) if no contraindication.
4. Gel heel pads or off-the-shelf orthoses; night splint if morning pain dominant.
5. Not improving at 6–12 weeks: physiotherapy; corticosteroid injection (e.g. methylprednisolone 20–40 mg with lidocaine) — short-term benefit only, risk of fat-pad atrophy and fascia rupture; extracorporeal shockwave therapy (NICE IPG311) via MSK service.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Routine podiatry/MSK referral if no improvement after 3–6 months of conservative care, or diagnostic uncertainty.
2. Orthopaedic/foot & ankle referral if symptoms >12 months despite the above; surgery (plantar fascia release) is a last resort.
3. Urgent: suspected stress fracture (offload, X-ray; MRI if X-ray normal), or features of inflammatory arthritis → rheumatology.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Plantar fasciitis, 2024)

options.label: Diagnosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Core features: age ≥50, bilateral shoulder ± pelvic girdle aching >2 weeks, morning stiffness >45 min, raised ESR/CRP, rapid (≥70%) response to prednisolone 15 mg within 1 week.
2. Before steroids: FBC, ESR + CRP, U&E, LFT, calcium, ALP, TSH, CK, RF, anti-CCP, urine dip, protein electrophoresis/light chains; chest X-ray if indicated.
3. ALWAYS ask about GCA: headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms → see Giant cell arteritis (same-day). Atypical features (age <60, no girdle pain, normal inflammatory markers, prominent peripheral synovitis, poor steroid response) → consider RA, myositis, malignancy, infection, hypothyroidism → rheumatology.

options.label: Treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Prednisolone 15 mg once daily (12.5–25 mg range); review at 1 week — expect dramatic improvement; if <70% improvement, reconsider diagnosis before escalating.
2. Taper (CKS): 15 mg for 3 weeks → 12.5 mg for 3 weeks → 10 mg for 4–6 weeks → then reduce by 1 mg every 4–8 weeks (or alternate-day reductions) to zero; typical course 1–2 years. Relapse: return to previous effective dose.
3. Bone protection from the start: alendronic acid 70 mg weekly + calcium/vitamin D (DEXA if <65 and no fracture). Gastroprotection (lansoprazole 15–30 mg od) if NSAID/high risk. Steroid card; sick-day rules.
4. Monitor: ESR/CRP, glucose/HbA1c, BP, weight every 3 months; warn about adrenal suppression on withdrawal.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same-day: any GCA feature.
2. Rheumatology (routine/urgent as clinically indicated): age <60, atypical features, poor or incomplete response to 15 mg, unable to reduce below 10 mg after 1 year, ≥2 relapses, steroid toxicity — consider methotrexate as steroid-sparing (specialist).

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Polymyalgia rheumatica, 2024; BSR 2015)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute hot swollen joint, typically knee or wrist in older adult; may follow illness/surgery. Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray supports but does not confirm. Definitive: aspiration — positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.
2. A hot swollen joint is SEPTIC ARTHRITIS until proven otherwise — same-day aspiration before any steroid; admit if unwell.
3. Screen for causes if <60 or polyarticular: calcium, PTH (hyperparathyroidism), ferritin/transferrin saturation (haemochromatosis), magnesium, ALP, TSH.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Rest, ice, aspiration (therapeutic).
2. NSAID: naproxen 500 mg bd or ibuprofen 400–600 mg tds with PPI, for shortest duration; OR colchicine 500 micrograms bd–qds (max 6 mg/course; reduce in renal impairment, interactions with statins/clarithromycin); OR intra-articular corticosteroid (methylprednisolone 40 mg) once infection excluded — preferred in elderly/renal impairment/anticoagulated.
3. Short oral prednisolone 15–20 mg for 3–5 days if the above are unsuitable.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: possible septic arthritis, unable to aspirate in primary care.
2. Rheumatology: recurrent attacks (consider colchicine 500 micrograms od–bd prophylaxis), chronic CPP inflammatory arthritis, young onset, metabolic cause found.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Gout — differentials; EULAR CPPD 2011/2023)

options.label: Suspected new RA
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
2WW rheumatology if persistent synovitis. Check RF, anti-CCP, CRP, FBC, U&E, LFT. Start DMARD within 3 months. NICE NG100.

options.label: DMARD choice
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
First-line: methotrexate 15 mg weekly (folic acid 5 mg weekly). Add sulfasalazine or hydroxychloroquine if MTX incomplete. Monitor FBC, LFT, creatinine. NICE NG100.

options.label: Acute flare
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Short-term prednisolone (e.g. 15 mg OD reducing over 3 weeks). Do not use long-term steroid without DMARD. NICE NG100.

options.label: Recognise
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute (<2 weeks) hot, swollen, painful joint with restricted movement, ± fever — in a prosthetic joint, immunosuppressed, diabetic, IV drug user, or elderly, fever and leucocytosis may be ABSENT.
2. Any acutely hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise (mortality ~10%, cartilage destroyed within days). Gout/pseudogout can co-exist with infection.

options.label: Action
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. SAME-DAY admission (orthopaedics/ED). Do NOT start antibiotics in primary care before joint aspiration and blood cultures unless the patient is septic and transfer is delayed.
2. Secondary care: aspiration (Gram stain, culture, crystals), blood cultures, FBC, CRP, urate; IV flucloxacillin (or per local policy/MRSA risk) for 2 weeks then oral, total 4–6 weeks; washout.
3. Prosthetic joint: never aspirate in primary care — urgent orthopaedic referral.

options.label: Follow-up
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. After discharge: complete antibiotic course, monitor CRP, physiotherapy to restore range; review risk factors (diabetes control, skin infections, immunosuppression).

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS — hot swollen joint; BSR/BOA hot swollen joint guideline)

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Emergency: Hot swollen joint – aspirate (send for MC&S), admit for IV antibiotics and washout. Do not delay. NICE NG100.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Age 40–60; global restriction of ACTIVE and PASSIVE movement, external rotation most limited; three phases — painful (2–9 months), stiff (4–12 months), thawing (12–42 months).
2. X-ray to exclude glenohumeral OA and posterior dislocation (both mimic). Check HbA1c and TFTs (diabetes ×5 risk; thyroid disease).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Explain natural history (most recover over 1–3 years; residual stiffness in some). Keep using the arm within pain.
2. Painful phase: paracetamol + ibuprofen 400 mg tds/naproxen 500 mg bd short course; intra-articular glenohumeral corticosteroid injection (methylprednisolone 40 mg or triamcinolone 40 mg, ideally image-guided) gives the best early pain relief; short oral prednisolone course only in exceptional cases.
3. Stiff phase: physiotherapy — stretching within pain, pulley/pendulum exercises; avoid aggressive manipulation.
4. Optimise diabetic control.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Refer orthopaedics/MSK if severe pain and loss of function unresponsive to injection + physiotherapy at 3–6 months: options hydrodilatation, manipulation under anaesthesia, arthroscopic capsular release (UK FROST: similar outcomes at 1 year — shared decision).
2. Diagnostic doubt (e.g. young patient, trauma) → imaging/referral.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Shoulder pain — frozen shoulder, 2024)

options.label: Red flags / urgent
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute trauma + loss of ACTIVE abduction/external rotation with preserved passive range → suspected acute full-thickness cuff tear: urgent X-ray and orthopaedic referral within 2–3 weeks (repair outcomes fall after 3 months), especially age <65.
2. Trauma + deformity/loss of rotation → X-ray same day (fracture, dislocation). Unreduced posterior dislocation is easily missed.
3. Systemically unwell, red hot joint → septic arthritis (same-day admission). Unexplained mass, night pain, weight loss, history of cancer → 2WW / urgent imaging.
4. Chest pain, pain unrelated to movement → consider cardiac or diaphragmatic/referred cause.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Painful arc 60–120°, pain on resisted abduction/external rotation, positive Hawkins–Kennedy → rotator cuff tendinopathy/subacromial pain. Weakness out of proportion → tear.
2. Global loss of passive external rotation → frozen shoulder or glenohumeral OA (X-ray distinguishes). Pain at ACJ with high-arc pain → ACJ.
3. Imaging: plain X-ray if trauma, age >60 with new symptoms, or not improving at 6–12 weeks. USS for suspected tear (via MSK service).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Education: most subacromial pain improves over 6–12 months; keep moving within pain; modify overhead work.
2. Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g qds; ibuprofen 400 mg tds or naproxen 500 mg bd short course (with PPI if risk); topical NSAID.
3. Physiotherapy: structured rotator-cuff and scapular strengthening ≥12 weeks is first-line.
4. Subacromial corticosteroid injection (e.g. methylprednisolone 40 mg + 1% lidocaine 4–5 ml, or triamcinolone 40 mg) for pain limiting rehabilitation; benefit ~6–8 weeks; maximum 2 injections, ≥6 weeks apart; avoid if tear suspected in young patient.
5. Calcific tendinopathy: same conservative care; USS-guided barbotage or ESWT via MSK service if persistent.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. MSK interface/physio-led service: not improving after 12 weeks of rehabilitation, or after 1–2 injections.
2. Orthopaedics: symptomatic full-thickness tear (especially traumatic, age <65), failure of 6 months conservative care (consider subacromial decompression — only after conservative care and shared decision; NICE/BESS), recurrent calcific deposits.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Shoulder pain, 2024; BESS/BOA)

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Refer rheumatology for diagnosis (clinical + ANA, dsDNA, complement). Treat flares per specialist. NICE CKS.

options.label: Red Flags (Cauda Equina / Malignancy)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica, night pain, weight loss, history of cancer. Urgent same-day referral/A&E. NICE NG59.

options.label: Stable / Spondylosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
Keep active. NSAIDs (regular) for flare. Physiotherapy referral. Avoid imaging in non-specific low back pain. Reassure if no neurology. NICE NG59.

tools.title: Stress fracture

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Insidious activity-related bone pain after a training increase; focal bony tenderness (stress fracture) vs diffuse posteromedial tibial tenderness over ≥5 cm (medial tibial stress syndrome).
2. Risk: female athlete triad/RED-S (ask about menstrual history, energy intake), low vitamin D, osteoporosis, long-term steroids, eating disorder, prior stress fracture.
3. X-ray first (often normal for 2–3 weeks); if normal and suspicion persists → MRI. High-risk sites needing urgent care: femoral neck, anterior tibial cortex, navicular, 5th metatarsal base, talus, sesamoid.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Low-risk sites (posteromedial tibia, 2nd–4th metatarsal shaft, fibula): offload — reduce impact, walking boot/stiff shoe if painful walking, cross-train (swim/cycle) 4–8 weeks, graded return when pain-free.
2. Medial tibial stress syndrome: relative rest 2–6 weeks, ice, calf/foot intrinsic strengthening, footwear/orthoses, gradual return (<10% weekly load increase).
3. Analgesia: paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs long term (may impair bone healing).
4. Bone health: check vitamin D and replace; calcium intake; address RED-S/menstrual dysfunction (sports dietitian, gynaecology); DEXA if recurrent.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Urgent orthopaedics: high-risk site, displaced fracture, inability to weight-bear, femoral neck pain in a runner (non-weight-bearing immediately).
2. Sports medicine/physiotherapy for return-to-sport planning; endocrinology/bone clinic if recurrent or low bone density.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS — sports injuries; BJSM bone stress injury consensus)

aliases: Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) – Management

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Mid-portion (2–6 cm above insertion, fusiform swelling) vs insertional (at calcaneus, often Haglund's). Morning stiffness, pain on loading.
2. Exclude rupture: Simmonds/Thompson test, palpable gap, sudden 'kick' sensation → see Achilles rupture.
3. Risk factors to address: fluoroquinolones (stop and avoid), corticosteroids, hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes, sudden training increase.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Relative rest (reduce not stop); ice after activity; heel raise/cushioned shoe; avoid flat shoes and hill running.
2. Progressive loading: eccentric heel-drop programme (Alfredson, 3×15 reps bd, 12 weeks) for mid-portion; floor-level only for insertional. Expect 3–6 months.
3. Analgesia short term: paracetamol; ibuprofen 400 mg tds ≤2 weeks.
4. DO NOT inject corticosteroid into or around the tendon (rupture risk).
5. Persisting >3 months: physiotherapy review; ESWT (NICE IPG312) via MSK service.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same-day orthopaedics/ED: suspected rupture.
2. Routine orthopaedic (foot & ankle) referral if no improvement after 6 months of a supervised loading programme; USS/MRI to characterise.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Achilles tendinopathy, 2024)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Pain and tenderness over lateral epicondyle, worse on resisted wrist/finger extension (Cozen's test) and gripping. No imaging needed for typical presentation.
2. Exclude: radial tunnel syndrome (pain 3–5 cm distal, worse resisted supination), cervical radiculopathy C6/7, elbow OA or loose body (locking), referred shoulder pain.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Explain: self-limiting, 90% settle in 6–24 months. Modify or pause the provoking activity; check ergonomics/grip size.
2. Analgesia: paracetamol; topical NSAID (ibuprofen 5% gel qds) first line; oral ibuprofen 400 mg tds for short courses only.
3. Physiotherapy: progressive loading/eccentric wrist extensor exercises for ≥6–12 weeks; counterforce (epicondylar) brace for symptom relief.
4. Corticosteroid injection: short-term relief only and WORSE outcomes at 6–12 months — not routinely recommended; consider only for severe pain limiting work/function after shared decision.
5. Avoid repeated injections; no evidence for PRP in routine care.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Routine MSK/orthopaedic referral if persistent >6–12 months despite loading programme, or diagnostic uncertainty (consider USS/MRI).
2. Surgical options (release/debridement) only after failed conservative care.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS Tennis elbow, 2024)

options.label: Mild to Moderate (Sensory only / Nocturnal symptoms)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN (Specialist Care):
1. Primary: Targeted corticosteroid injection (e.g. 20-40mg Methylprednisolone) into carpal tunnel. Highly effective for symptom relief.
2. Splintage: Mandatory neutral-angle nocturnal wrist splints for 8 weeks.
3. Neuro-monitoring: Repeat NCS in 3-6 months if persistent. NICE CKS.

options.label: Severe (Motor deficit / Thenar atrophy)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN (Surgical Care):
1. Gold Standard: Open or endoscopic Carpal Tunnel Release (CTR).
2. Urgency: Required within 4-8 weeks to prevent irreversible axotomy/atrophy.
3. NCS Findings: Expect prolonged distal motor latency (DML > 4.5ms) and absent/reduced amplitudes.

options.label: Painful (subacute / De Quervain's thyroiditis)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Often viral; self-limiting. NSAID for pain; beta-blocker if thyrotoxic symptoms. Monitor TFTs (may go through thyrotoxic then hypothyroid phase).
2. Refer if severe, prolonged, or diagnostic uncertainty. NICE NG145, CKS.

options.label: Painless / postpartum
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Monitor TFTs (may fluctuate). Treat hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism as per NICE NG145. Postpartum: often resolves; recheck at 6 months. NICE CKS.

tools.title: Are we doing enough chest X-rays in primary care – Management

options.label: When to request
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Unexplained cough >3 weeks, haemoptysis, suspected cancer, pneumonia, pleural effusion, suspected TB, or red flags. NICE NG12, NG120.

tools.title: Asthma

options.label: Step 1: SABA prn
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Indication: Symptoms < 3 times/week and no night-waking.
2. Warning: If using SABA ≥3 times/week, move to Step 2. BTS/SIGN Guidelines.

options.label: Step 2: Low-dose ICS
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. 1st-line: Beclometasone (e.g. Clenil 100mcg bd). Prevents airway remodelling and reduces exacerbation risk. BTS/SIGN.

options.label: Step 3: Add LABA (Combined Inhaler)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. 1st-line: ICS + LABA (e.g. Fostair or Symbicort). MART (Maintenance and Reliever Therapy) is the specialist preference for improved adherence.
2. Review: If still poorly controlled on moderate-dose ICS+LABA, consider LTRA (Montelukast). BTS/SIGN.

options.label: Moderate (PEFR 50-75% best)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Treatment: SABA 2-5 puffs via spacer every 10-20 mins. Oral Prednisolone 40-50mg for 5 days. BTS/SIGN.

options.label: Severe (PEFR 33-50% / RR ≥ 25 / HR ≥ 110)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Triage: Immediate hospital admission (999). High-flow Oxygen. Nebulised SABA + Ipratropium. BTS/SIGN.

options.label: Life-Threatening (PEFR <33% / SpO2 <92% / Silent Chest)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Emergency: 999. Do not delay. Life-threatening features (33-92-CHEST). BTS/SIGN.

aliases: Asthma diagnosis and treatment  what's changed in the 2024 BTS, NICE and SIGN guideline – Management
Asthma treatment, monitoring and self-management  what's changed in the 2024 BTS, NICE a – Management

options.label: Stable Management (BTS Guidelines)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Airway Clearance: Mandatory referral to Respiratory Physio for techniques (ACBT). Regular exercise.
2. Vaccination: Annual Flu + Pneumococcal.
3. Sputum: Send for culture (ensure no Pseudomonas/Haemophilus colonization). BTS Guideline, NICE CKS.

options.label: Exacerbation
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Treatment: 14 days of Targeted Antibiotics (based on previous sputum cultures). Start Amoxicillin or Doxycycline if no previous culture.
2. CT: HRCT Chest is required for definitive diagnosis. BTS Guideline, NICE CKS.

options.label: Safe for Home
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN (RCPCH):
1. Hydration: Ensure ≥ 50-75% normal fluid intake. Check for ≥2 wet nappies in 12h.
2. Admission: Refer if SpO2 < 92% (in air), RR > 70, or apnea reported.
3. No Meds: Do not use inhalers, steroids, or antibiotics. NICE NG9 / RCPCH.

options.label: Refer to Hospital
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Indication: RR > 70, saturations < 92%, apnoeas, or persistent reduced feeding (<50%).
2. Action: Urgent Paediatric referral. NICE NG9.

options.label: Suspected OSA (NICE NG202)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Score: Use **Epworth Sleepiness Scale** (>10 is abnormal).
2. Risk: Assess for comorbidities (BMI >30, HTN, Diabetes).
3. Referral: Sleep clinic for Nocturnal Oximetry or Polysomnography.
4. Driving: Advise patient to inform DVLA if excessive daytime sleepiness affects driving. NICE NG202.

options.label: LAMA+LABA (Dual Therapy)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN (Consultant Plan):
1. First-line for patients with persistent breathlessness or exacerbations despite SABA/LAMA mono.
2. Inhalers: e.g. Anoro Ellipta, Ultibro Breezhaler, Spiolto Respimat.
3. Action: Check technique; offer Pulmonary Rehab if MRC ≥ 2. NICE NG115.

options.label: Triple Therapy (LABA+LAMA+ICS)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN (Consultant Plan):
1. Indication: Blood eosinophil count ≥ 0.3 x10^9/L OR ≥ 1 severe / 2 moderate exacerbations per year.
2. Inhalers: Trelegy Ellipta or Trimbow.
3. Risk: Discuss increased risk of pneumonia with ICS use. NICE NG115.

options.label: Refractory / Advanced COPD
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Chronic Macrolide: Consider Azithromycin 250mg tiw if non-smoker and frequent exacerbations (requires baseline ECG & LFT).
2. Oxygen: Assess for LTOT (Long Term Oxygen Therapy) if pO2 < 7.3 kPa stable.
3. Referral: Lung volume reduction or Transplant assessment. NICE NG115.

options.label: Exacerbation / when to refer
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Moderate: Increase SABA; add prednisolone 30 mg 5–7 days; consider antibiotic if purulent sputum.
2. Admit: Severe (respiratory failure, confusion, cyanosis), or poor response. NICE NG115, CKS.

tools.title: Cough – acute bronchitis, post-viral and chronic cough

options.label: Acute cough / bronchitis (<3 weeks)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Usually viral; self-care — honey (>1 year), fluids, paracetamol/ibuprofen, pelargonium/guaifenesin optional; cough lasts 3–4 weeks. NG120: NO antibiotic for acute bronchitis in otherwise well adults/children; consider immediate or back-up antibiotic if systemically very unwell, high risk of complications (≥65 with ≥2 of hospitalisation last year, diabetes, heart failure, oral steroids; or ≥80 with ≥1), or symptoms worsening rapidly: doxycycline 200 mg day 1 then 100 mg od for 5 days (adults); amoxicillin 500 mg tds 5 days (children/pregnancy); clarithromycin/erythromycin if allergic. CRP point-of-care if available (<20 no antibiotic; 20–100 back-up; >100 immediate).
2. Pneumonia (CRB-65, focal signs, saturations <95%, RR >24, HR >100, fever >38 with crackles) → amoxicillin 500 mg–1 g tds 5 days (doxycycline/clarithromycin if allergic); admit if CRB-65 ≥2, saturations <92%, or unable to cope. Whooping cough (paroxysms, whoop, vomiting, ≥2 weeks; contact with cases; infants) → notify, PCR/serology, clarithromycin/azithromycin if within 3 weeks of onset (limits spread), exclude 48 h; vaccinate pregnant contacts.
3. Safety-net: haemoptysis, chest pain, breathlessness, weight loss, cough >3 weeks → reassess.

options.label: Chronic cough (>8 weeks) — work-up
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Red flags → CXR and 2WW lung cancer if ≥40 with ≥2 of (or ≥1 if smoker): cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss; haemoptysis ≥40 → 2WW regardless; persistent chest infection, finger clubbing, supraclavicular/persistent cervical nodes, thrombocytosis → urgent CXR (NG12).
2. All chronic cough: CXR, spirometry with reversibility (± FeNO), stop ACE inhibitor (switch to ARB — cough resolves within 4 weeks), stop smoking/vaping, review occupational/environmental exposure, assess for the 'big three': asthma/eosinophilic bronchitis (variable, nocturnal, FeNO/eosinophils → ICS trial 8 weeks), upper airway cough syndrome/rhinitis (post-nasal drip, throat clearing → intranasal steroid + antihistamine 4–8 weeks), GORD (heartburn, worse after meals/lying → PPI 8-week trial only if reflux symptoms; lifestyle). Also: bronchiectasis (sputum — HRCT), TB (risk factors, sputum AFB), OSA, heart failure (BNP), interstitial lung disease (crackles, clubbing — HRCT), pertussis.
3. Trial treatments sequentially for 4–8 weeks each; stop if no effect.

options.label: Refractory / unexplained chronic cough
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. If CXR, spirometry normal and treatment trials fail: 'cough hypersensitivity syndrome' (often women 50–60, laryngeal irritation, triggers — talking, cold air, perfume). Refer respiratory/specialist cough clinic (HRCT, bronchoscopy, methacholine challenge, oesophageal pH/manometry as needed).
2. Non-drug: speech and language therapy cough-suppression/laryngeal hygiene programme (first line, good evidence), hydration, avoid throat clearing, honey/lozenges.
3. Neuromodulators (specialist-led/off-label): low-dose morphine MR 5–10 mg bd (best evidence, constipation), gabapentin 300 mg → up to 1800 mg/day or pregabalin, amitriptyline 10–25 mg nocte; gefapixant (P2X3 antagonist — NICE TA1024 approved 2024 for refractory chronic cough after specialist assessment). Avoid codeine linctus/dextromethorphan long term.

curated.by: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

options.label: Assessment & referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. LTOT: Assess when stable on optimal treatment; pO2 <7.3 kPa (or <8 with complications). Refer respiratory for assessment. NICE NG115.

options.label: Pleural effusion
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. CXR; consider tap for diagnosis. Light's criteria. Refer if exudate, malignant, or symptomatic. NICE CKS.

options.label: Haemoptysis / cancer
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Haemoptysis: 2WW lung cancer. Cough: no antibiotic for acute bronchitis; consider asthma/ACE-i. Pulmonary nodule: refer per NICE. NICE NG12, NG120.

options.label: Suspected ILD (Persistent Crackles)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN (Consultant Plan):
1. Presentation: Progressive SOB + dry cough + 'velcro' fine crackles on auscultation. No infective signs.
2. Workup: CXR (may be normal early), Spirometry (restrictive pattern), HRCT Chest.
3. Referral: Urgent Respiratory referral if fibrosis suspected. NICE NG105.

tools.title: Less common respiratory diagnoses – sarcoidosis, aspergillosis, CTEPH, diaphragm paralysis, neuromuscular respiratory failure

options.label: Sarcoidosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Presentations: incidental bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) on CXR; Löfgren's syndrome (BHL + erythema nodosum + ankle arthritis + fever — excellent prognosis, no biopsy needed); dry cough/breathlessness; skin (lupus pernio, papules, scar sarcoid); eyes (uveitis — urgent ophthalmology); cardiac (palpitations, syncope, heart block — ECG/Holter/MRI); neuro (facial palsy, meningitis); hypercalcaemia/renal stones; fatigue.
2. Work-up: CXR (Scadding stage), FBC, U&E, calcium, LFT, serum ACE (non-specific), ECG, urinalysis, spirometry/gas transfer, TB screen (IGRA — exclude mimic), HRCT; refer respiratory for diagnosis (EBUS lymph node biopsy — non-caseating granulomas) and staging; ophthalmology slit-lamp for all at diagnosis.
3. Treatment (BTS 2020): most stage I–II need observation only (resolves in 60–80% within 2–5 years). Prednisolone 20–40 mg daily tapering over 6–12 months for: symptomatic/progressive pulmonary disease, cardiac, neuro, ocular (not responding to topical), hypercalcaemia, severe skin, renal; methotrexate/azathioprine as steroid-sparing; infliximab refractory (specialist). GP: bone protection with steroids, monitor calcium (avoid vitamin D supplements unless deficient — hypercalcaemia), vaccinations, fatigue management, NSAIDs for Löfgren's; monitor CXR/spirometry 3–6 monthly in first 2 years.

options.label: Aspergillosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. ABPA (asthma/CF with worsening control, brown plugs, fleeting infiltrates, eosinophilia, total IgE >1000 IU/mL, Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG, bronchiectasis central): refer respiratory; prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg 2 weeks then taper over 3–6 months ± itraconazole 200 mg bd 16 weeks (steroid-sparing; LFT/ECG QT, many interactions — statins, DOACs, some antihistamines); monitor IgE; optimise asthma (biologics — omalizumab/mepolizumab — in severe cases).
2. Aspergilloma (fungal ball in a pre-existing cavity — old TB, sarcoid, emphysema; CXR 'air crescent'): often asymptomatic; HAEMOPTYSIS can be massive → same-day admission if significant; options — observation, itraconazole/voriconazole (limited benefit), bronchial artery embolisation for bleeding, surgical resection if fit and recurrent haemoptysis. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (cavitation, weight loss, Aspergillus IgG) — long-term azole via respiratory/ID.
3. Invasive aspergillosis (neutropenia, transplant, ITU/COVID/flu): fever + nodules/halo on CT → urgent haematology/ID (voriconazole IV).

options.label: CTEPH, diaphragm paralysis, neuromuscular respiratory failure
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. CTEPH: persistent breathlessness/exercise intolerance ≥3 months after PE on anticoagulation (or history of VTE, pacemaker, splenectomy, thrombophilia); loud P2, RV heave, raised JVP; echo (RVSP >35–40 mmHg) + V/Q scan (preferred screening) → refer pulmonary hypertension centre (Papworth/Hammersmith/Sheffield/Newcastle/Glasgow/Great Ormond St/Royal Free — right heart catheter, CT pulmonary angiography). Treatment: lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin preferred by many centres; DOAC acceptable), pulmonary endarterectomy (potentially curative), balloon pulmonary angioplasty, riociguat (NICE TA). GP: avoid pregnancy (high mortality — contraception advice), oxygen if hypoxic, vaccinations, avoid high altitude.
2. Diaphragm paralysis: orthopnoea, breathlessness on bending/immersion, paradoxical abdominal movement; causes — phrenic nerve (tumour, trauma/surgery, neuralgic amyotrophy, cervical spondylosis, MND, viral), idiopathic. CXR (raised hemidiaphragm) → sniff test (fluoroscopy/USS), spirometry sitting vs supine (>20–25% fall), CT chest for cause. Unilateral: often tolerated — reassure, weight loss, treat cause; bilateral → respiratory failure (nocturnal hypoventilation — overnight oximetry/capnography) → NIV via home ventilation service; diaphragm plication (thoracic surgery) if symptomatic unilateral.
3. Neuromuscular respiratory failure (MND, muscular dystrophy, myasthenia, GBS, post-polio, SMA, high spinal cord injury): symptoms — orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness, poor cough, recurrent chest infections, unexplained weight loss; monitor FVC (sitting and supine) and SNIP every 3 months in MND; refer home ventilation/respiratory neuromuscular service when FVC <80% predicted, orthopnoea, or symptomatic for NIV, cough assist (mechanical insufflation-exsufflation), secretion management; vaccinations; early palliative/advance care planning; ACUTE deterioration (FVC <1–1.5 L, cannot count to 20, swallowing failure) → 999 (ITU).

options.label: 2WW referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Haemoptysis; CXR suggestive; persistent cough with red flags. Refer via 2WW. NICE NG12.

tools.title: Lung cancer pathway – incidental nodules, mediastinal mass, metastases, mesothelioma

options.label: Incidental pulmonary nodule (BTS)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Solid nodule <5 mm (or <80 mm³) → no follow-up (very low risk); 5–6 mm (80–300 mm³) → CT at 1 year (then discharge if stable volume); 6–8 mm or ≥300 mm³ → CT at 3 months then 1 year (volumetry — volume doubling time); ≥8 mm (≥300 mm³) → Brock risk model: <10% → CT surveillance; ≥10% → PET-CT ± biopsy via lung MDT. Sub-solid/ground-glass nodules: CT at 3 months, then annually for 4 years if persistent (slow-growing adenocarcinoma spectrum).
2. In practice: the reporting radiologist usually states the BTS pathway — ensure the follow-up CT is booked (safety-net tracker); refer lung MDT/respiratory for any nodule ≥8 mm, growth, spiculation, upper-lobe location with risk factors, or patient anxiety needing discussion. Explain risk honestly (most nodules benign — granuloma, hamartoma, intrapulmonary node).
3. Multiple nodules (≥5) in a patient with known cancer → metastases until proven otherwise (oncology); in infection/immunosuppressed → fungal/septic emboli/TB (respiratory).

options.label: Suspected lung cancer, mediastinal mass, metastases
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG12: 2WW if CXR suggests lung cancer or age ≥40 with unexplained haemoptysis. Urgent CXR (within 2 weeks) if ≥40 with ≥2 of cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss (≥1 if ever-smoker), or persistent/recurrent chest infection, clubbing, supraclavicular/persistent cervical nodes, thrombocytosis, chest signs. Normal CXR does not exclude cancer — persistent symptoms → CT/2WW.
2. Mediastinal mass on CXR (widened mediastinum, hilar enlargement): CT chest with contrast urgently; anterior — thymoma/teratoma/thyroid/lymphoma ('4 Ts'), middle — lymphadenopathy (lymphoma, sarcoid, TB, metastatic), posterior — neurogenic; superior vena cava obstruction (facial/arm swelling, distended neck veins, headache) → same-day oncology/ED (steroids, stenting, radiotherapy). Myasthenia symptoms → thymoma.
3. Lung metastases (cannonball/multiple nodules): common primaries — colorectal, breast, renal, bladder, melanoma, sarcoma, germ cell, thyroid, head & neck; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, tumour markers as indicated, refer to the relevant site MDT (or acute oncology if unknown primary — 2WW 'non-specific symptoms' pathway). Targeted Lung Health Checks (England): low-dose CT for ever-smokers 55–74 — encourage uptake; eligibility via GP record search.

options.label: Mesothelioma
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Asbestos exposure (shipyards, construction, plumbing, electricians, laggers — often 20–50 years prior, including secondary/household exposure): chest pain (often dull, non-pleuritic), breathlessness, unilateral pleural effusion, weight loss, pleural thickening/plaques on CXR. Any pleural effusion/thickening + asbestos history → 2WW respiratory/pleural MDT (CT, thoracoscopic biopsy).
2. Specialist: chemotherapy (pemetrexed + platinum; nivolumab + ipilimumab first line — NICE TA818), IPC/pleurodesis for effusion, radiotherapy for pain/tract sites, surgery rarely; median survival ~12–18 months; early palliative care; Mesothelioma UK nurse.
3. GP: breathlessness/pain management (opioids, neuropathic agents for chest wall invasion), psychological support, notify (reportable to coroner at death — industrial disease), help with compensation: Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit (100% automatic), Diffuse Mesothelioma Payment Scheme/2008 scheme (DWP), civil claim via specialist solicitor (time limits — 3 years from diagnosis), War Pension if forces; document exposure history carefully.
